purpose: Individually calibrate all 43 science cards remaining in the v323 hand-picked legacy-core candidate samples after v324/v326/v327/v328, across Physics and teacher-taught Chemistry.
source: v323 live mock-core audit minus exact IDs already reviewed in v324, v326, v327 and v328

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: A projectile has initial horizontal velocity 12 m s⁻¹. Without air resistance, what is its speed at the highest point?
records.originalBack: 12 m s⁻¹.
accept: At maximum height its vertical speed is zero, so its total speed is the unchanged 12 m s^-1 horizontal speed.
reject: Its speed is 0 m s^-1 at the highest point.
Its speed rises above 12 m s^-1 at the highest point.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Which wave property stays unchanged across a stationary boundary?
records.originalBack: Frequency.
accept: The wave frequency remains the same when it passes into a different medium.
reject: The wavelength always stays the same when a wave enters a different medium.
The speed always remains unchanged as a wave crosses into another medium.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Why does the photoelectric effect contradict the simple classical wave model?
records.originalBack: Emission has a threshold frequency and no significant delay above it, even at low intensity.
accept: There is a threshold frequency and prompt emission even for low intensity light above that threshold.
reject: Increasing intensity at any frequency eventually emits photoelectrons.
Very low-intensity light above threshold must first accumulate energy for a long delay.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How do you calculate the maximum speed of emitted photoelectrons?
records.originalBack: Find Eₖ(max) = hf − φ in joules, then use vₘₐₓ = √(2Eₖ(max)/mₑ).
accept: First find hf minus the work function, then calculate v = sqrt(2(hf - phi)/me) using energies in joules.
reject: Maximum electron speed equals (hf - phi) divided by electron mass.
Use sqrt(2hf/me), ignoring the metal work function.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How much energy does one photon transfer to one electron in the photoelectric effect?
records.originalBack: hf.
accept: One photon delivers energy E = h f to an electron.
reject: The transferred photon energy is hf minus the work function.
The energy transferred by one photon is h/f.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is the quark–antiquark content of anti-K⁰?
records.originalBack: s + anti-d.
accept: One strange quark and one anti-down quark.
reject: One down quark and one anti-strange quark.
One strange quark and one anti-up quark.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Define a baryon.
records.originalBack: A hadron made from three quarks; an antibaryon has three antiquarks.
accept: A baryon is a hadron containing three quarks.
reject: A baryon contains one quark and one antiquark.
A baryon is a hadron containing two quarks and one lepton.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: Which baryon is stable in the AQA particle classification?
records.originalBack: The proton; other baryons eventually decay.
accept: The stable baryon is the proton.
reject: The free neutron is the only stable baryon.
The lambda baryon is the stable baryon.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: What is the derived SI unit of resistivity?
records.originalBack: Ohm metre (Ω m).
accept: Resistivity has SI unit ohm metres, Ω m.
reject: The SI unit is ohms per metre, Ω/m.
The SI unit of resistivity is ohm metres to the power minus one.

records.subject: Physics
records.originalFront: How is wire cross-sectional area obtained from diameter d?
records.originalBack: A = πd²/4.
accept: Use A = pi(d/2)^2, where d is the diameter.
reject: The cross-sectional area is A = pi d^2.
The cross-sectional area is A = 2 pi d.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How does first ionisation energy change down Group 2?
records.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: The first ionisation energy generally falls down Group 2 because shielding and atomic radius increase.
reject: The first ionisation energy increases steadily down Group 2.
The first ionisation energy is constant down Group 2.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the purpose of a chemical test for an organic group?
records.originalBack: To identify a functional group by a characteristic observation.
accept: Identify a functional group from a characteristic chemical reaction and observation.
reject: The test determines only the exact relative molecular mass of the organic compound.
The test always reveals the entire carbon skeleton without further information.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the Arrhenius plot gradient for ln k against 1/T?
records.originalBack: −Ea/R.
accept: The slope of ln k against inverse temperature is negative activation energy divided by R.
reject: The gradient of ln k against 1/T is +Ea/R.
The gradient of ln k against 1/T is -R/Ea.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: In a Born–Haber cycle, define first ionisation energy.
records.originalBack: Energy required to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms, forming gaseous 1+ ions.
accept: One mole of gaseous atoms each loses one electron to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
reject: It is the energy to remove a second electron from one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
It is the energy released when gaseous 1+ ions gain an electron.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: When does entropy usually increase?
records.originalBack: When particles become more dispersed/disordered, especially when more gas particles are formed.
accept: Entropy generally rises when there are more gas particles and greater dispersal of energy and matter.
reject: Producing more gas particles always lowers entropy.
Changing a gas into a solid usually raises entropy.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.section: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
records.originalFront: What is Ka?
records.originalBack: The acid dissociation equilibrium constant.
accept: Ka is the equilibrium constant for HA dissociating into H+ and A- in solution.
reject: Ka is the rate constant for acid dissociation.
Ka is the ionic product of water.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.section: Strong weak acids pH Ka Kw
records.originalFront: Why are carboxylic acids weak acids?
records.originalBack: They only partially dissociate in water.
accept: Carboxylic acid molecules ionise only partly in aqueous solution.
reject: Carboxylic acids fully dissociate in water.
They are weak only because their solutions are always dilute.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How can proton transfer assist an alcohol elimination mechanism?
records.originalBack: It changes –OH to a better leaving group and permits catalyst regeneration.
accept: Protonation changes -OH into an -OH2+ group so that water can leave, with acid regenerated.
reject: Proton transfer converts -OH into O2- to make it a better leaving group.
Protonating an alcohol prevents water from leaving.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What happens in elimination from a halogenoalkane?
records.originalBack: H and a halogen leave, creating a C=C bond.
accept: A hydrogen and halogen are removed from neighbouring carbons, producing an alkene double bond.
reject: The halogen is replaced by OH to form an alcohol.
Elimination removes a C=C bond and creates a saturated carbon chain.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the main type of product from nucleophilic substitution by OH⁻?
records.originalBack: An alcohol.
accept: A halogenoalkane undergoes substitution by hydroxide to form an alcohol.
reject: Nucleophilic substitution by OH- yields a ketone.
Nucleophilic substitution by OH- gives an alkene by loss of HX.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is an oxidising agent?
records.originalBack: Species that accepts electrons and is reduced.
accept: An oxidising agent accepts electrons and is itself reduced.
reject: An oxidising agent donates electrons and becomes oxidised.
An oxidising agent always increases its own oxidation state.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Which is the stronger oxidising agent: chlorine or bromine?
records.originalBack: Chlorine.
accept: Chlorine, Cl2, is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.
reject: Bromine is the stronger oxidising agent.
Chlorine and bromine have exactly equal oxidising strengths.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: How does oxidising strength change down Group 7?
records.originalBack: It decreases.
accept: Oxidising power decreases from chlorine to bromine to iodine.
reject: Oxidising strength increases down Group 7.
The oxidising strength of the halogens does not vary down the group.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why can some carbonyl additions create enantiomer pairs?
records.originalBack: Attack from opposite faces of the planar carbonyl creates different configurations.
accept: Nucleophiles can attack either face of a planar carbonyl, producing mirror-image products if a new chiral centre forms.
reject: A carbonyl can only be attacked from one face, so only one configuration is formed.
The carbonyl carbon is already tetrahedral, preventing opposite-face attack.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why does a racemic mixture give no net optical rotation?
records.originalBack: The enantiomers' rotations cancel.
accept: Equal amounts of opposite enantiomers rotate plane-polarised light by equal and opposite angles, giving zero net rotation.
reject: A racemic mixture has no optical rotation because every molecule is achiral.
The enantiomers in a racemic mixture both rotate light the same way.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is a chiral centre?
records.originalBack: Usually a carbon bonded to four different groups.
accept: A typical chiral centre is a tetrahedral carbon attached to four different substituents.
reject: A carbon joined to four identical groups is a chiral centre.
Any carbon atom double-bonded to oxygen is automatically a chiral centre.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the functional group in a ketone?
records.originalBack: Carbonyl group between two carbon atoms.
accept: A ketone contains R-C(=O)-R' with carbon groups on both sides of the carbonyl carbon.
reject: A ketone always has a terminal -CHO group.
The ketone functional group is -COOH.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What forms when a ketone is reduced?
records.originalBack: A secondary alcohol.
accept: Reduction of a ketone produces a secondary alcohol.
reject: Reducing a ketone produces a primary alcohol.
Reducing a ketone produces a tertiary alcohol.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What forms when an aldehyde is reduced?
records.originalBack: A primary alcohol.
accept: Reduction of an aldehyde produces a primary alcohol.
reject: Reducing an aldehyde produces a secondary alcohol.
Reducing an aldehyde produces a tertiary alcohol.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why is a carboxylic acid described as weak?
records.originalBack: Only a fraction of its molecules dissociate into ions in water.
accept: Carboxylic acids are weak because most molecules remain undissociated in water at equilibrium.
reject: They are weak because they completely ionise in water.
They are weak only because the acid solution must be dilute.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why do carboxylic acids react with carbonates?
records.originalBack: Their acidic protons react with carbonate ions, releasing carbon dioxide.
accept: An acid reacts with a carbonate to produce a carboxylate salt, water and carbon dioxide.
reject: Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to release hydrogen gas rather than carbon dioxide.
A carbonate reaction with a carboxylic acid produces chlorine gas.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What numbering rule applies when naming a carboxylic acid?
records.originalBack: The carbon in –COOH is carbon number 1.
accept: The carboxyl carbon in the COOH group is carbon 1.
reject: Number the carbon next to COOH as carbon 1, ignoring the carboxyl carbon.
Always start numbering from the far end away from COOH.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is the ester functional group?
accept: An ester has the linkage R-C(=O)-O-R'.
reject: An ester has the functional group R-COOH.
An ester has the functional group R-CONH2.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What does an acyl chloride contain?
records.originalBack: The –COCl functional group.
accept: The acyl chloride functional group is R-C(=O)-Cl.
reject: An acyl chloride has the -COOH functional group.
An acyl chloride contains -COOR rather than -COCl.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What acyl product forms when an acyl chloride reacts with ammonia?
records.originalBack: A primary amide.
accept: An acyl chloride plus ammonia forms RCONH2, a primary amide.
reject: Reaction with ammonia gives an ester RCOOR'.
Acyl chloride plus ammonia forms only an N-alkyl amide RCONHR'.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What acyl product forms when an acyl chloride reacts with a primary amine?
records.originalBack: An N-substituted amide.
accept: An acyl chloride and a primary amine form an N-substituted amide RCONHR'.
reject: Reaction with a primary amine forms the unsubstituted amide RCONH2 only.
The acyl product is an ester RCOOR'.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why are acyl chlorides more reactive than amides?
records.originalBack: Chloride is a much better leaving group.
accept: Chloride is a better leaving group than amide, making acyl chlorides more readily substituted.
reject: The -NH2 group is a much better leaving group than chloride.
Acyl chlorides are less reactive because their chlorine cannot leave.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Which acid-derived groups are joined to glycerol in a triglyceride?
records.originalBack: Three long-chain fatty acid residues.
accept: A triglyceride has glycerol esterified with three long-chain fatty acid residues.
reject: Glycerol in a triglyceride is linked to three amino-acid residues.
A triglyceride contains only one fatty acid residue joined to glycerol.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Can a triglyceride contain three different fatty acids?
records.originalBack: Yes. The three long chains need not be identical.
accept: Yes, each ester-linked fatty acid chain can be different.
reject: No, triglycerides must have three identical fatty acid chains.
A triglyceride can have only two fatty acid chains.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is saponification?
records.originalBack: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats or oils.
accept: Saponification is base hydrolysis of fats or oils to glycerol and fatty acid salts.
reject: Saponification is acid-catalysed esterification making triglycerides.
Saponification is oxidation of fats to form ketones.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: Why does soap clean oily substances?
records.originalBack: Its non-polar tail interacts with oil and its ionic head with water.
accept: The non-polar hydrocarbon tail associates with oil and the hydrophilic ionic head stays in water, allowing micelles.
reject: The ionic soap head dissolves in oil and the hydrocarbon tail dissolves in water.
Soap cleans oil by reacting to release oxygen gas.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: What is AQA Required Practical 2 about?
records.originalBack: Measuring an enthalpy change using calorimetry.
accept: AQA Required Practical 2 uses temperature changes and calorimetry to measure an enthalpy change.
reject: Required Practical 2 determines reaction rate from gas volume against time.
Required Practical 2 determines Mr by mass spectrometry.

records.subject: Chemistry
records.originalFront: A thermometer is ±0.1°C per reading. What is the uncertainty in ΔT?
records.originalBack: ±0.2°C: add the absolute uncertainties of initial and final readings.
accept: Plus or minus 0.2 degrees Celsius, since uncertainty in the two readings is added.
reject: The total uncertainty in the temperature difference is only plus or minus 0.1 degrees Celsius.
Uncertainty in the temperature change is plus or minus 0.01 degrees Celsius.

limitations: This is a curated 43-card correction, not full AQA assessable-bullet certification.
Unseen user answers can still expose marker mistakes.
All original question text, answers, card IDs and progress storage stay unchanged.
